extracted.intended_audience: aspiring amateur stand-up comedians and general readers interested in live comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing for and delivering a short (club) stand-up comedy set as an amateur, with focus on stagecraft, material delivery, time management, and coping with nerves. The guidance is from a first‑person account of doing a six‑minute club set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing/visual neutrality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice from a more experienced comedian: wear plain clothes (the author wore a plain grey T‑shirt, 'the least funny shirt I owned') so your costume doesn't become a distraction or attempt at a visual joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap/crass/shocking laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't go for the easy crass laugh; don't confuse shocking with funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tony's explicit advice: avoid crude shock value as the primary tactic. The piece warns that amateurs often try shock which can backfire and cheapen the set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't memorise verbatim
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't memorise your material: Know what you want to say, but not how to say it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: 'That’s how amateurs usually trip themselves up — they recite rather than perform, and if they miss a line or even a word, the rest of their bit can vanish from them like dreams.' The recommendation is to internalize ideas and beats rather than exact wording so you can adapt mid‑set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice/experience yields looseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Looseness and ease onstage come from practice; experienced performers have a looseness amateurs lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed contrast in the club: a performer who had been up before 'had the looseness that only practice can bring.' Implication: rehearse and get stage time to build natural delivery and presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: MC framing affects audience reception
rubrics_metrics.description: MC telling the crowd you are a newbie can soften the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: the MC introduced the author as a newbie and 'that sometimes softened things up.' Use MC introductions strategically (they can lower expectations and make audiences more forgiving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management and red‑light / time limit awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of club time warnings: the red light at 5.5 minutes and a strict six‑minute cutoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venue mechanics matter: know where you are in your set relative to the warning and cutoff so you can wrap a joke or tag and avoid being cut off ('After five and a half minutes onstage, I’d see a red light go on. That was my warning. At six minutes, one way or another, I was done').

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage entrance and mic handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Mind your entrance, body onstage, and how you handle the mic and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details from the account: walk onto stage confidently, pull the microphone from the stand, move the empty microphone stand to the back, and be aware of lighting (the bright stage light can be blinding). Small physical actions (where you place the stand, how you hold the mic) contribute to presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pauses and breathing for timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pauses and breathing affect laughter; strategic pauses can increase audience response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Whenever I pause to come up for air, there’s a little more laughter.' Guidance: use pauses to give the audience space to react and to control pacing rather than rushing through lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to improvise but expect limited windows
rubrics_metrics.description: If lines aren't working, consider improvising, but opportunities to pivot may pass quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's reflection: 'Some lines that seemed funny on the page aren’t working out loud, and I think I should improvise... but those windows streak by like highway exits, too late to turn around.' Practical advice: practice having fallback bits or tags and be alert to quick decisions on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test material — page vs. stage difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that reads well on the page may not work when performed aloud; test and adapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit observation: 'Some lines that seemed funny on the page aren’t working out loud.' Guidance: try material in front of people (open mic, friends) and revise for live rhythm and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental framing: keep perspective on short set
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt perspective that a short set is temporary: 'It’s six minutes of your life. What’s the worst that can happen?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing helps manage nerves and fear. The MC and friends also provided pep talks; using mental minimization can reduce pressure and help performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savouring and recognizing earned laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when you 'earn' laughter and let it affect your confidence and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes a moment of relief when he hears real laughter: 'That’s laughter ... and I earned it. It’s mine to keep. I feel my shoulders relax.' Guidance: notice audience responses and use them to build momentum rather than rushing on.
